locator: Results > Ketamine in Haloperidol-Treated Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 12); Table 2, BPRS Total Score and BPRS Psychosis Subscale rows (p. 13)
extracted: Twenty minutes after the injection, on haloperidol, the BPRS total was 33.4 (6.0) after salt water and 38.3 (7.1), 39.3 (5.0) and 45.3 (7.7) after 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 mg/kg, significant at 0.3 (p = .005) and 0.5 mg/kg (p = .01), against baselines of 34.6 (7.0), 33.2 (4.2), 35.2 (5.4) and 36.9 (11.0); n = 9, 9, 9 and 7. The three psychosis items carried the change: 8.0 (3.1) after salt water against 9.8 (3.3) (p = .05), 9.3 (2.8) and 12.3 (2.5) (p = .02), from baselines of 8.1, 6.8, 6.6 and 6.9. At 90 and 180 minutes the total is at or below its own baseline in every condition (at 0.5 mg/kg, 32.3 and 32.3), while the psychosis score at 0.1 and 0.3 mg/kg is 7.0 at both times, just above baselines of 6.8 and 6.6, and Table 2 marks the 0.1 mg/kg value at 180 minutes significant although it sits below the salt-water value of 7.9. The paper nowhere says whether the figures in brackets are standard deviations or standard errors; they make sense only as standard deviations. No test statistic, degrees of freedom, interval or effect size is printed.

locator: Abstract, last third (p. 9); Results > Ketamine in Haloperidol-Treated Subjects, last paragraph (p. 12); Table 3, column heading 'Delayed Drug Effects' and its entries (p. 14)
extracted: The paper gives the timing of the later reports in three incompatible ways: the abstract calls them delayed or prolonged effects at 8 to 24 hours, the results say the delusions came back about 6 to 8 hours after the injection, and the heading of the table that lists them per person reads 4 to 24 hours, while that table's own entries record one episode lasting 12 hours, dreaming over two nights and visual phenomena recurring over several days. Nothing in the paper reconciles the three windows.

locator: Results, 1st paragraph (left column) continuing in the right column; Figure 1
extracted: Free recall of a 12-word categorical list was lower on the ketamine day than on the salt-water day in 15 healthy volunteers: drug F1,14 = 9.63 (p = .008), time F4,56 = 5.16 (p = .005), drug x time F4,52 = 4.35 (p = .004); lower at 55 minutes F1,13 = 18.79 (p = .001) and at 90 minutes F1,13 = 6.25 (p = .026). Recognition of the same words (n = 14) was lower too: drug F1,13 = 17.48 (p = .001), time F4,52 = 6.05, drug x time F4,52 = 7.95 (p < .001), lower at 10 minutes F1,13 = 8.92 (p = .01) and 55 minutes F1,13 = 18.78. The attention score fell less markedly: drug x time F4,56 = 2.71 (p = .05), lower at 55 minutes only, F1,14 = 8.79 (p = .01). The paper's individual counts at 55 minutes of the ketamine infusion are falls from each person's own pre-infusion level on that day, not differences from the salt-water day: 13 of 15 for free recall, 9 of 14 for recognition and 9 of 15 for attention. All three measures come from the same word list, so they are not independent of each other.

locator: Methods > Clinical Assessments, paragraph on the BPRS, continuing at the top of p. 109 (pp. 108-109); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 114)
extracted: For the BPRS hallucinatory-behaviour item, which is one of the three items of the positive subscale, the authors used the original, wider item description so that perceptual distortions as well as hallucinations could be scored on it, so this study's positive-subscale scores are not comparable with studies that score that item in the usual way and the rise cannot be read as evidence of hallucinations. In the Discussion the authors state that the study did not detect formal thought disorder or language disorganisation during the conditions tested, apart from modest effects on the alogia subscale of the negative-symptom scale, although blocking, loosening of associations and language disorganisation were noted during the loading period.
